title: 1 Chronicles 25:1–8
context: As part of David’s preparations for the temple, the families of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun are set apart to prophesy with instruments in the LORD’s house. Their 288 skilled singers are assigned duties by lot, small and great alike.

verses.text: Moreover, David and the captains of the army set apart for the service certain of the sons of Asaph, of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who were to prophesy with harps, with stringed instruments, and with cymbals. The number of those who did the work according to their service was:
verses.arminianNotes: David and the army captains set apart sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun “to prophesy with harps, with stringed instruments, and with cymbals.” Arminian readers see gifted people called and organized to lead Israel’s worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s ordering of worship through David’s arrangements. The link between prophecy and music suggests Spirit-led praise; readers in this tradition note 1 Samuel 10:5 and 2 Kings 3:15 without defining the practice precisely.

verses.text: of the sons of Asaph: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asharelah. The sons of Asaph were under the hand of Asaph, who prophesied at the order of the king.
verses.arminianNotes: The sons of Asaph serve “under the hand of Asaph, who prophesied at the order of the king.” Arminian readers see willing service within an ordered structure, with leaders and learners working together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see authority and order in worship. Asaph’s name is attached to Psalms 50 and 73–83, and readers in this tradition value the link between these musicians and the psalms Israel sang.

verses.text: Of Jeduthun, the sons of Jeduthun: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Shimei, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six, under the hands of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied in giving thanks and praising the LORD with the harp.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeduthun’s six sons serve under their father, “who prophesied in giving thanks and praising the LORD with the harp.” Arminian readers see thanksgiving and praise as the heart of this ministry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see prophecy expressed through thanksgiving and praise. The name Jeduthun appears in the titles of Psalms 39, 62, and 77, connecting this family with Israel’s worship songs.

verses.text: Of Heman, the sons of Heman: Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel, Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, Romamti-Ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, and Mahazioth.
verses.arminianNotes: Heman’s fourteen sons are named. Arminian readers see a family devoted to God’s service across a generation. Some interpreters have suggested the later names may form a phrase of praise, though this remains a proposal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s blessing on Heman’s household. The long list honors each individual, and readers in this tradition hold any proposed meaning in the names lightly, since the text does not explain them.

verses.text: All these were the sons of Heman the king’s seer in the words of God, to lift up the horn. God gave to Heman fourteen sons and three daughters.
verses.arminianNotes: Heman is “the king’s seer in the words of God,” and “God gave to Heman fourteen sons and three daughters.” Arminian readers see family blessing received as God’s gift and returned in service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s gift of children credited directly to him. The phrase “to lift up the horn” is not explained fully, and readers in this tradition generally take it as exalting or strengthening, while holding the exact sense loosely.

verses.text: All these were under the hands of their father for song in the LORD’s house, with cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps, for the service of God’s house: Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman being under the order of the king.
verses.arminianNotes: They serve “for song in the LORD’s house, with cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps,” under their fathers and the king. Arminian readers see music offered as real service to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see worship carried out in an ordered way. Both traditions commonly value music in worship, and readers in this tradition note that this verse describes temple arrangements without settling later debates about instruments.

verses.text: The number of them, with their brothers who were instructed in singing to the LORD, even all who were skillful, was two hundred eighty-eight.
verses.arminianNotes: The number of skilled singers with their brothers is 288. Arminian readers see training and skill valued, as people developed their gifts for God’s service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see skill in worship as fitting for God’s house. The number corresponds to twenty-four groups of twelve, matching the lots that follow in verses 9–31.

verses.text: They cast lots for their offices, all alike, the small as well as the great, the teacher as well as the student.
verses.arminianNotes: “They cast lots for their offices, all alike, the small as well as the great, the teacher as well as the student.” Arminian readers see fairness, with no one favored by status or skill.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the lot as a way of receiving assignments from God, in keeping with Proverbs 16:33. The equal treatment of teacher and student shows that service is assigned, not earned by rank.
